description: Reflection, refraction at boundaries, and how converging and diverging lenses form images.
content_html:
Reflection at Plane Surfaces

When a wave strikes a smooth, flat surface, it is reflected. The key rule is that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection — both angles are measured from the normal, which is an imaginary line at right angles to the surface at the point of contact.

The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane. During reflection, the wave speed, frequency and wavelength all remain unchanged — only the direction of travel changes. A plane (flat) mirror forms a virtual image: the image appears to be behind the mirror, is the same size as the object, is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, and is laterally inverted (left and right swapped).

Key Fact

Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both from the normal). During reflection, wave speed, frequency and wavelength are unchanged. A plane mirror produces a virtual image the same size as and the same distance from the mirror as the object.

Refraction at Boundaries

Refraction occurs when a wave crosses the boundary between two media with different optical densities. The wave changes speed, and if it hits the boundary at an angle (not along the normal), it also changes direction.

The rules of refraction are:
• When a wave passes from a less dense medium into a denser medium (e.g. air into glass), it slows down and bends towards the normal.
• When a wave passes from a denser medium into a less dense medium (e.g. glass into air), it speeds up and bends away from the normal.
• The frequency stays the same at both sides of the boundary. The wavelength changes because \(\lambda = \frac{v}{f}\) and the speed changes.

Different wavelengths of light refract by different amounts when entering glass. Violet light slows more than red light, causing the colours to spread. This is how a prism separates white light into its spectrum.

To draw a refraction ray diagram correctly:

1. Draw the boundary between the two media (e.g. air and glass) as a solid line.
2. Draw the normal at the point of incidence — a dashed line at 90° to the boundary.
3. Draw the incident ray and label the angle of incidence (\(i\)) from the normal.
4. Draw the refracted ray on the other side of the boundary. If the ray enters glass from air, it bends towards the normal; the angle of refraction (\(r\)) is smaller than \(i\).
5. If the ray exits glass into air, it bends away from the normal; \(r > i\).
6. Label both media and indicate the direction of travel with arrows.

Lenses — Converging and Diverging

Lenses work by refracting light at two curved surfaces. There are two types:

A converging lens (convex lens) is thicker in the middle. Parallel rays of light passing through it bend and converge at the focal point on the far side. The distance from the lens centre to the focal point is the focal length.

A diverging lens (concave lens) is thinner in the middle. Parallel rays passing through it spread apart (diverge) and appear to come from a focal point on the same side as the incoming light.

Key Fact

Converging (convex) lens: thicker in the middle; parallel rays meet at the focal point. Diverging (concave) lens: thinner in the middle; parallel rays spread apart, appearing to come from a focal point on the same side as the light source.

To draw a converging-lens ray diagram, use three principal rays from the top of the object:
1. A ray parallel to the principal axis → refracts through the far focal point.
2. A ray through the optical centre of the lens → passes straight through without bending.
3. A ray through the near focal point → refracts to travel parallel to the principal axis.

The image depends on the object’s distance from the lens (measured in multiples of the focal length \(f\)):

Object beyond 2f: the image is real, inverted and diminished (smaller than the object). This is how a camera forms an image on its sensor.

Object at 2f: the image is real, inverted and the same size as the object, formed at 2f on the other side.

Object between f and 2f: the image is real, inverted and magnified (larger than the object). This is how a projector works.

Object closer than f: the refracted rays diverge and do not meet on the far side. When extended back, they appear to come from a point on the same side as the object — a virtual, upright and magnified image. This is how a magnifying glass works.

A real image is formed where light rays actually meet. It can be projected onto a screen. Images formed by converging lenses when the object is beyond the focal point are real.

A virtual image is formed where rays appear to come from when extended backwards — no light actually passes through the image position. It cannot be projected onto a screen. The image in a plane mirror and the magnifying glass image are both virtual. Virtual images are always upright; real images are always inverted (for a single converging lens).

The power of a lens is defined as \(P = \frac{1}{f}\), where \(f\) is the focal length in metres and power \(P\) is measured in dioptres (D). A short focal length means a high-power (strongly converging) lens. For a diverging lens, the focal length is negative, so the power is negative. Opticians prescribe spectacle lenses in dioptres: a \(+2\) D lens has a focal length of 0.5 m; a \(-4\) D lens has a focal length of −0.25 m.
exam_tip_html: Ray diagram questions are often worth 3–4 marks. You must draw all three principal rays accurately and clearly mark the image where two or more rays meet (or appear to meet). Label the image as real/virtual, upright/inverted and magnified/diminished/same size — all three descriptors earn marks. For refraction, always draw the normal first as a dashed line perpendicular to the boundary, then state which way the ray bends and why. A common error is bending the ray the wrong way — remember: slowing down = bends towards the normal.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (from the normal); speed, frequency and wavelength unchanged. Plane mirror image is virtual, same size and distance.
  • Refraction: wave slows and bends towards the normal entering a denser medium; speeds up and bends away when leaving. Frequency constant; wavelength changes.
  • Converging lenses form real, inverted images when the object is beyond the focal point; a virtual, magnified image when the object is within one focal length (magnifying glass effect). Diverging lenses always form virtual, upright, diminished images.

practice_questions.text: State what happens to the speed of a light ray when it passes from air into glass.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the speed decreases (light slows down in glass compared to air).

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the focal point of a converging lens.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the point on the principal axis where parallel rays of light converge after passing through the lens. 1 mark: located on the far side of the lens from the incoming light, at a distance equal to the focal length.

practice_questions.text: A converging lens has a focal length of 0.2 m. An object is placed 0.5 m from the lens. Without drawing a diagram, state whether the image formed is real or virtual, and state whether it is upright or inverted.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: real image (object is beyond the focal point). 1 mark: inverted (real images from a single converging lens are always inverted).

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the idea of refraction, why a glass prism splits white light into a range of colours.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains that white light is made up of different wavelengths (colours); different wavelengths travel at different speeds in glass so they refract by different amounts; violet light refracts more than red light, causing the colours to spread out and form a spectrum. Secure: states different colours refract by different amounts in glass, producing a spectrum. Developing: states the prism separates colours but does not explain why different colours refract differently. Emerging: mentions refraction without linking it to wavelength or colour.

practice_questions.text: An object is placed between the focal point and the lens of a converging lens. Which of the following best describes the image formed?
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: Virtual, upright and magnified. Distractors: Real, inverted and magnified; Real, inverted and diminished; Virtual, inverted and diminished.

practice_questions.text: Draw and describe the ray diagram for a converging lens forming a real image of an object placed beyond twice the focal length. Include the three principal rays, label the image, and describe its characteristics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: draws all three principal rays correctly (parallel ray through far focal point; central ray straight; near-focal-point ray emerging parallel); rays converge to form image beyond 2f on the far side; image correctly labelled as real, inverted, diminished; diagram is neat with principal axis, lens, both focal points and object labelled. Secure: draws two or three rays with minor errors; image correctly placed with two characteristics stated. Developing: one ray correct; image placed approximately correctly; at least one characteristic stated. Emerging: lens and focal points drawn but ray paths largely incorrect.

knowledge_checks.q: A ray of light passes from glass into air. Which direction does it bend relative to the normal?
Which type of lens is used as a magnifying glass?
options: Diverging lens with object beyond focal point
Converging lens with object beyond focal point
Converging lens with object inside the focal point
Diverging lens with object inside the focal point

knowledge_checks.q: When drawing a ray diagram for a converging lens, a ray that passes through the optical centre of the lens continues _____.
A virtual image _____ be projected onto a screen.
Match each situation to the type of image formed by a converging lens.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the law of reflection?
flashcard_questions.a: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (both measured from the normal).
The change in speed (and direction) of a wave as it crosses a boundary between two media.

flashcard_questions.q: When a light ray enters glass from air, which way does it bend?
When a light ray leaves glass into air, which way does it bend?
flashcard_questions.a: Away from the normal (it speeds up).
A lens thicker in the middle that brings parallel rays to a focal point.
A lens thinner in the middle that causes parallel rays to spread apart.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the focal point of a lens?
flashcard_questions.a: The point where parallel rays meet (or appear to come from) after passing through the lens.

flashcard_questions.q: A converging lens forms a magnified virtual image when the object is _____ the focal length.
What type of image does a plane mirror form?
flashcard_questions.a: A virtual, upright image the same size as and same distance from the mirror as the object.

flashcard_questions.q: State one property that real images have but virtual images do not.
flashcard_questions.a: A real image can be projected onto a screen.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a glass prism split white light into colours?
flashcard_questions.a: Different wavelengths refract by different amounts in glass.

flashcard_questions.q: What quantity stays the same when a wave is refracted at a boundary?
flashcard_questions.a: Frequency — it does not change at a boundary.

glossary_terms.definition: An imaginary line drawn perpendicular to a surface at the point where a wave or ray meets it; angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal.
The change in direction (and speed) of a wave as it passes from one medium into another with a different optical density.
A lens that is thicker in the middle than at the edges; parallel rays passing through it converge at the focal point on the far side.
A lens that is thinner in the middle than at the edges; parallel rays passing through it diverge, appearing to come from a focal point on the same side as the incoming light.
The point at which parallel rays converge after passing through a converging lens, or from which they appear to diverge after a diverging lens.
